notes.meaning: The Lord speaks as the true King and commander over all armies, declaring doom against Moab. Prominent Moabite cities like Nebo and Kiriathaim will be captured, ruined, and disgraced. Their strong highland fortresses will be pulled down, showing that human defenses cannot stop God's judgment.

Moab will no longer have reason to boast of its greatness or renown. In Heshbon, the invading Babylonians devise plans to wipe out Moab so that it stops being an independent nation. Other towns like Madmen will be silenced as the enemy sword pursues their citizens.

Loud cries of terror and ruin rise from the city of Horonaim. The invading army brings total destruction as it sweeps through the region. It shows that no corner of Moab will be spared from the coming storm.

The entire nation of Moab is shattered and defeated. Even the little children cry out in helplessness and fear as violence overtakes their homes. The suffering reaches everyone in the land, from the greatest leaders to the smallest children.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the Hebrew word for 'little ones' as the nearby city Zoar, following the ancient Greek translation and matching parallel prophetic passages.

notes.meaning: Refugees flee along the mountain roads, weeping continually as they climb the slope up to Luhith. On the descent toward Horonaim, agonized screams ring out over the devastation of their cities. Whether climbing or descending, the people find nothing but grief and peril.

The people are urged to run for their lives and leave all their belongings behind. They must become like a solitary, stripped bush in the barren desert to avoid the advancing troops. In times of supreme crisis, preserving life is far more important than clinging to earthly possessions.

Moab felt secure because of its wealth, strong fortifications, and devotion to its national god Chemosh. Yet these false confidences will completely fail when the conquerors arrive. The idol of Chemosh will even be hauled off into exile alongside its own priests and rulers.

The Babylonians will move like a destroyer against every single city without letting one town escape. Both the low valleys and the fertile plateau regions of Moab will be ruined. This sweeping collapse is certain because the Lord Himself has declared it.

Moab faces such sudden devastation that its cities will be emptied of all their people. The danger is so urgent that the Moabites would need wings like a bird to have any hope of escape. The once-crowded land is sentenced to total desolation.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Based on ancient language parallels, some modern translations render the opening phrase as spreading salt over Moab to mark its barrenness and destruction.

notes.meaning: God warns the invading soldiers to carry out His decree of judgment thoroughly and without holding back. Failing to perform the Lord's appointed work or being careless with the sword brings a curse upon the conqueror. God uses earthly armies as instruments of His justice, and His purpose cannot be done halfway.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators view this verse as a traditional military proverb or an exaggerated saying about complete judgment rather than a literal command for cruelty.

notes.meaning: Moab is compared to wine that has sat undisturbed on its dregs without being strained from vessel to vessel. Because the nation had lived in long peace and avoided exile, it grew complacent, proud, and lazy. Its sinful nature remained untamed because it had never faced the refining trials of other nations.

The Lord declares that Moab's unbroken ease will come to a sudden end. He will send Babylonian invaders like rough wine-workers to tip Moab over and empty the nation into captivity. They will pour out the inhabitants and shatter their proud cities like fragile clay jars.

Moab will be deeply disappointed and ashamed when Chemosh proves unable to rescue them from destruction. This mirrors the northern kingdom of Israel, who foolishly trusted the golden calf at Bethel only to be carried off by Assyria. Idols always fail and leave their worshippers disgraced in the day of trouble.

The Lord directly challenges the proud boast of Moab's soldiers who claim to be mighty champions ready for battle. They trusted in their military strength, body armor, and martial skill. In the day of God's judgment, human might cannot stand against His purpose.

Moab is shattered as foreign troops invade its cities and put down its best young warriors in battle. This downfall is guaranteed by the true King of creation, the Lord of Hosts. His supreme power far exceeds that of any earthly king or warrior.

The disaster facing Moab is not far away in the distant future; it is rushing toward them quickly. Though the nation felt safe behind its borders, the divine sentence was already in motion. When God's judgment is set, it arrives with unstoppable speed.

Surrounding nations and all who knew Moab's former glory are called to weep over its sudden collapse. The royal scepter and staff, representing Moab's authority and dominion, have been completely broken. The overthrow of a proud empire serves as a sober warning to all its neighbors.

The proud royal city of Dibon is commanded to step down from its seat of honor and sit on parched ground in total disgrace. Though Dibon enjoyed abundant water and strong fortresses, the Babylonian destroyer will pull down every defense. Pride and luxury will quickly be traded for thirst and humiliation.

The people of Aroer, living along the northern border road, are told to stand and watch for travelers. They must ask fleeing men and women what terrible news has happened in the heart of the country. The sight of refugees running for survival reveals that Moab's defenses have completely fallen.

The fleeing refugees answer that Moab is utterly humiliated and broken into pieces. A bitter cry of lament is to be sounded all along the Arnon River, the nation's key boundary. The message that the entire country has been laid waste must be proclaimed everywhere.

God's judgment reaches across the high plateau, striking every single town in its path. Cities like Holon, Jahzah, Mephaath, Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim are listed one by one as they fall to the enemy. This detailed list shows that God's justice is thorough and overlooks no part of the rebellious land.

The disaster spreads through Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon, Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the other towns of Moab. Whether a city is near the border or hidden deep in the country, none will escape the coming destruction. All earthly strongholds must yield when the Lord brings His righteous judgment.
